text.p:
I hope Cous: Roger will be got safe to Rydal long here this comes, and I wish you could find him answer ire hopes, and ye time and charges expended here. But his Genius leading him some other
way, you will judge it most advisable otherwise to bestow him. His Brother is more tractable and Studious now he is alone. In their accounts (which I send) you will observe their battles are lowered considerably, though still but too high; and I believe ire Son will own where ye fault was, yt they have hitherto been so extravagant. The debt you mentioned to be discharged is brought in at 3£. 10s. 6d; which is so unreasonable, that I told the man that trusted them, I would never enter any Such bill in my accounts, nor so far countenance Such practices; and if he be made to wait for his money, it is too small a punishment for what is past, and may in great measure prevent ye like for ye future. Notwithstanding if you send it up, it shall be paid and all possible care taken to amend that fault. My Service and respects as due. I am

note.value: 623. JAMES FLEMING TO ROGER FLEMING.

text.p:
After so long a absence, a Letter would be very acceptable; I
cannot imagine ye reason of it; your business cannot be so great, but you may have one hour at com~and; I would gladly be informed with ye news country; and what is remarkable since your departure, is as follows; The last night, Dr Pennington & my Worship, had ye happiness to drink a glass with Mr Bones after ye Gates at his chamber, who drunk your health over and over, and returned thank for our company, and would be glad of ye same opportunity. Likewise with Mr Sherlock and Mr Washington, who were all very well rounshoulderd before we parted; Yesterday buried Mr Auxlay his wife,
whose death is very much lamented; so has my showmaker; yett it's reported, that he makes love to Sew at ye Gray-Hound. Doctor Pudsday is married, as we hear, with ye Lady Willis; Mr Willis won ye plait in pourt-mead last Thursday, where a great many Scholars were gadered; But ye undergraduates of our house, were all welcomed home, with an imposition of 20 distich. Quo (i?) strepit in Campo hic silent in Schools. Jaky Brougham is here, who designs to tarry ye vacation, as we suppose. Mrs Min has an elder sister come home, who excels her, as much as Katarine; As concerning ye business with
Tom Manners, and Adam Kantwell, remains un don; I desired it to be don, who promised, yett not so soon, least it should be ye reason of an other engagement. This night Mr Smith jur having his name stopped for Mr Dayle, for absenting prayers ye Horse-Race night, carried him an epistle, which proved to be ye same with one of yours, which you & Huchinson had translated into Greek, so how he comes of I cannot as yett tell. Mr Huchinson is gon into ye country for a quarter of
a year. Mr Brougham finding you sessed in Tom: Burneat's row, asked how it came; ye Senior answered that you told Tom of it, that he might take of you as of ye rest, so Mr Brougham was well satisfied; Yett as soon as ever I heard of it, I acquainted Mr Brougham with it, and told him you were gone into ye country before Tom cam, so presently Relton was ordered to be put on for it. The money for ye bed acquoted Noas Ark, and for The hangings, which was much less than you thought of, was spent in your name, with those whom you entirely loved. Mrs Lauther is highly displeased at you, not for seeing her before your journey; Which makes me afraid to visit her. Cousings ye Under Cooke is gone from ye Coll: and in his place, Mr Provist put in ye Cook's Brother. Eastgate Jenny and her comrade is lately parted, and is gon to below ye Eastgate, where she has caused several to repent of their former extravigancus; The reason of this disagreement
is, as we gather from others, ye Morbus Gallicus. John Blackman, who lived at ye Coffy House, under ye East-gate, was brought in bed ye last week, which looked very suspicious upon her; After ye wives had been with her a long time, not thinking her to be with child (neither would she confess it) were going home, one of them thought she heard a child cry, which made them search ye bed, at which she was forced to confess; Several people thought it was not ye first time, that she had been in that condition; She had provided no cloose for ye child; so censure of it, as you think fit. Great water works are making here for ye good of ye City; pipes are and must be laid all over Oxon~. They are working to draw ye water from friar bacon study, which must furnish all ye pipes, a work worth any mans
observation. All ex Aula~ Edmundi are well. Mr Bird having no news to writ, begs your pardon to ye next opportunity. Pray pardon all faults
Dr Pennington gives his service particularly to you when you write any thing extrorny to me sent in a loose paper. For Mr Roger Fleming nigh Kendal, att Rydal By ye way of London

note.value: 624. ROGER FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: from Sum~erford bodes in Chesr. Aug. ye 25. 95. Sr

Having not heard any thing from you in all this time, makes me suppose yt my letters have miscarried, but ye reason why you have not writ, I think is, because you might expect me ere this, which I beg your pardon for so doing without your leve, but it hath been out of my power to come, which I am apt to think will be yet for some time,
for both my Cousin Swettenham and his Lady, are very unwilling to part with me till she be brought abed which is expected every day, for then he designs to give you a visit him self, which till then I desire your pardon if so be I cannot get away, which is all but my duty to you and love to my Brothers and Sisters from your
My Cousin and his Lady gives their service to you and the rest. ffor Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal Westmld

note.value: 625. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
What the affects of your last letter were, I have almost forgot; yett one thing I remember, which Mr Browham did not act according to (to quit the late extraviganc's) Upon two reasons, 1st because he had no money in his hand, and 2ly least two quick a payment should give encouragement to a future engagement, having nothing to write he gives his service to you; I have been a little uneasy for it, by ye next I hope to see it quited; As for lining I can dispense with it till ye next opportunity; I should think my self in your favour to be entrusted with some money to account for, which will prove both for
your profit,and my satisfaction; its my Tutor has it I know nothing what is disbursed, till he send you ye Accounts; My Bro: Goo: is very well, who is all ways ready to instruct me; My Service to all Bro: and Sisters, I am
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal nigh Kendal in Westmorland By way of London

note.value: 626. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I writ to my Brother Dan about 5 weeks since, but whether he hath received ye Letter or no, I know not, having not had an answer. Tom, Sr, I suppose will be with you very shortly, & therefore I must humbly beg you'll be pleased to contribute to my not only being here, but well being also; & what makes me the more ashur'd of your good affection in it, is the calling to mind a kind letter you sent me, before my leaving Oxford ye last time. The monies Sr you let me have at my coming last to Oxon, came short of what my necessities required, & therefore hope you will now double the sum~ you then were pleased to give me. Here hath been ye greatest canvassing for a New Major, yt hath been perhaps in ye memory of man; the Candidates purses bleeding as freely (as they call it here) as ever those who stood for
Burgasses for Clithero possibly could. But what Sr makes this office to be so courted now (a place formerly rather avoided then desired) is the stroke it gives in ye Election of Burgasses; for whether of ye opposite parties proved more numerous in Freemen, in ye Election of ye Major, in in all probability would be ye like in chewsing new Par. men. The E. of Abington & my Lt Wharton are ye chief of each party, and ye E. carried ye former, as also its supposed he'll do ye latter. Sr Will. Trumball its said will stand for ye Univ. Sr my
Bro. James is very well, & orderly & gives his duty to you, & wee both desire Sr your blessing. I am
Sr Your most obliged & obedient Son
Our Service Sr to all our Brothers & Sisters. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydal near Kendal in Westmerland These

note.value: 630. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO JAMES FLEMING.

text.p:
I have yours of ye 22th of ye last month, and I am very glad to hear that you are well. Your brother Roger is not yet come home, staying still with my Cousin Swettenham in Cheshire. He is so extravagant, the Lord only knows what will become of him. Wilful wast, makes woeful want; and debauched idle & ungodly Lives, too often occasion sad Exits. I am glad to hear that you have shaken off
some of your loose & idle comrades, that you are grown more civil, provident & studious, & that you'll be advised by your brother George & follow his Example. This will be much to your Honour, & will help you to preferment. My Cousin Henry Brougham is much in ye Right, not to be very quick in paying off such extravagant Ticks, least there should be more of them. I hope you'll have a care for ye Future, least you be ruined. Whilst you do well, I will do what I can for you: But if you do otherwise, you'll soon Repent it. I am sorry to hear, that you have almost forgot ye effect of my last Letter. When I was at Oxford, I used to be very careful of all my Fathers Letters; to be often reading of them; & to be very careful of obeying his commands; I also kept copies of all my Letters to him, that I might ye better remember what I writ to him, & perform what I promised him; And in these things, & in all other things that are good, it will not be amiss for you to follow your Fathers Example. When as I am well assured that trusting you with some money will not be for your & my prejudice, as it was in your brother Rogers case, I shall then be persuaded to it. The more you study, ye less you'll spend; and by your Expenses I shall ye best judge of your spending your Time. Fear God, & keep his commandments, & then all things will succeed well with you. My service to my Cousin Louder; & all other my good Friends. The Lord bless you. I am
Yours of July 16. 95 I have & I thank you for it & ye enclosed.

note.value: 632. REV. HENRY BROUGHAM TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: Yesterday, and not before, I was informed of my Cous: George's intention to go to ye East-Indies as Chaplain to a Merchant Ship. I have examined into ye thing as impartially as I can, and discoursed Several about it; and upon ye whole I look upon it to be one of ye most unaccountable projects that ever was Set a foot, considering his circumstances. It is great odds but he looses his life in ye voyage, or breaks his Constitution for ever: and besides the danger, there is neither Interest, improvement, or reputation to be got by it, as far as I can learn. I have endeavoured to break ye neck of it as much as I can; but may have got my Self ill will thereby: but Shall willingly bear with that, so I may discharge ye love and Service I owe him as a Relation & ffriend. And as such I take ye freedom to give my opinion, that if ever you made use of your autority over a child, it is now that ire com~ands should take place. He's not altogether so hot upon it as before; and if I had not been kept a Stranger to it, I think it should never have gone so far. I would be very sorry to obstruct any thing that might tend to his advantage; but this I think cannot prove so. If you are of another mind, I hope you will pardon ye good intention of
Dear Sr Ire most obedient Son & Servant
Cous. James go's better on with his Work, Since his Mate left him.
To Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal Westmrland to be sent with speed.

note.value: 634. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. GEORGE FLEMING.

text.p: I was very much surprised at ye Receipt of yours of ye sixth instant, & I am very much troubled that you should think of an East-Indian Voyage, which you fancy so Pleasant, and which is really so very dangerous & full of great hazards. I cannot give my consent to it, fearing that I shall then never see you more. I had much rather, that you should continue in ye University to improve your self in ye Ministry, & I doubt not but that you'll get better preferment. You'll want Books & good company abroad, & I think it will be 100. to 1. whether you'll return, and 1000 to 1. whether in such a condition as Mr Evens you mention. I believe ye Bishop will not give you leave to be so long absent; and have a care of losing ye Substance in catching at ye Shadow. I fancy your worthy good Friend Mr Principal will not advise you to this dangerous long Voyage, & I hope yt you'll well consider it before you Embark therein. It is not for you to turn Trader, that was never raised in it; you are not (God be praised) in a Desperate condition; therefore consider well of it & the Lord direct you in this & all other things; & the Lord bless you. I am

note.value: 635. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. HENRY BROUGHAM.

text.p:
Yours of ye 8th instant came yesterday unto my hand, for which I return you my most hearty thanks; and I am sure that both my son George & I are much obliged unto you for your good Advice unto him. Having lately received a Letter from him I writ by ye last Post: But
fearing that may miss of him, I shall here give you a copy of my Letter, which I desire you to show him, if he be yet in Oxford.

note.value: HERE FOLLOWS 634

text.p: I hope upon his Reading of this Letter, as he will not trouble himself with any more thoughts of an East-Indian Voyage, or of any such Extravagant Project. It is a great Folly (to say no worse) for a hopeful young Gentleman, against his Fathers Advice & Consent to hazard his Life, where there is neither Interest, Improvement, or Reputation to be got by it. Pray tell him, I am very hopeful, that what I have writ will be enough to dissuade him from such a fond undertaking; and if that will not do, I will add my com~ands thereunto. I believe not any of his Real Friends will advise him to it, nor, I think, any of his Relations. Pray continue to Advise him, & I am glad to hear well of my son James; But as to my Son Roger, he is not yet got hither. My service to all my good Friends with you. I shall ever remain,
Sr, Your most obliged & affectionate kinsman & servant
For Mr. Hen. Brougham at Oxon.

note.value: 637. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Yours by Tom came to my hand, & am glad to hear that you are well; This morning my Bro: George received a letter from my Bro: Michael at London, who designs ye next week to pay us a visit, if his business will permit him; Also from my Bro: Roger in Chessire, who is very well; what he proposes to himself in living so long with my Cos. Swetnam, I cannot imagine; my Cousin. Brougham of late hath been very much indisposed in health. That which is most remarkable
in Coll~ & University, has been ye Canvassing for Parliamt men; For ye University Sr Wm Trumble is chosen, whom Sr Chris. Musgrave opposed; For ye City Sr Edward Norris & Thomas Rowney Esq; For supplies of any necessities I can dispense with till ye next opportunity; My Sister Bosh sent me 5s by Tom; I desire you to return her thanks. I am
His Majesty is expected here very shortly. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydall These.

note.value: 638. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Yours by Tom, & the 30£ Pounds, I have received, & shall employ it as well, & putt it as far, as I possibly can. Here are great expectations from ye new Parliament, in which representatives for this Univ. are Sr Will. Trumbal ye P. Secret. & Mr Finch who was
a Burgess for us in ye last. In the City have been very great canvassing, but Sr Adieu. Norris, & Mr Rowney (who was H. Shir. of his County about 2 years agony) are elected, and we hear that in most other places hereabouts, those yt are firm to the Ch. and Gover. are elected. I have heard some say that being Chaplain to ye H. of Com~ons is accounted a good Post, you Sr must know whether its so or no; & if it be, I do not question your interest in procuring it for me. Dr Charlotte Master of Univ. Coll. hath expressed an extraordinary kindness for you; & thereupon gave me an invitation to stand this next week for a Fellow-ship there, but upon his further examining ye Statutes he found it inconsistent with any other preferment & so wee let it sleep, and desiring your Blessing I rest
Since my writing this, I have received a letter from the Captain, who is now in London, & will be in Oxon~ shortly. The King will be hear in his way to Windsor. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydal These.

note.value: 641. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Upon some late discourse with Mr Brougham concerning accounts I from his words conceive him to be disgusted & consequently perhaps to design & cause some difference between you & me; therefore I humbly present is not to prevent & praepossess you (though in reason I believe I could do it) with an opinion of my frugality, but by way of Vindication to what he shall allege agst me. It is an excellent rule which Seneca lays down that Queen statuit aliquid part inaudita~ altera~, aequu~ licit statuerit, haud aequus fuerit ; you have abundantly showed as well your knowledge as liking of it by your practise of it for many years; and I am better certified of your great love & tender kindness to me than to doubt or fear a due examination of both parties before condemnation of either. It may perhaps be a groundless surmise of mine, - his great indisposition of body may (as we com~only see it does) cause that most
pernicious passion of peevishness, whence might proceed our difference in stating accounts: if otherwise it behooves me in point of com~on prudence venienti occurrere morbo : I won't endeavour to clear my self from ye imputation of being very chargeable to you, time, place, & circumstances I hope will excuse this, but for any thing of extravagance I attest ye whole College, my former (except one) and even present account, which Mr Brougham sends impartialy to witness ye contrary. To insist more particularly upon ye last, for ye former bills are cordially examined & out of ye abundance of your fatherly kindness passed by and besid's I am more immediately concerned in this, I do with all submission offer this to your consideration, 1st ye inconvenience of ticking; for those who know before they must credit (perhaps for a pretty while) will without doubt exact, for conscience I am sure won't check those I am forced to deal with by Mr Broughams order: where such exaction is there must needs be large bills. 2ly ye neglect of paying & clearing accounts frequently. The more a snowball is rolled over, ye more still it contracts & grows ye larger even into a mountain: Thus a Tailor's (though perhaps Mr Bro: will take ye least notice of him, yet I am sure he deserves most) a shoemaker's, a glover's bill by continual addition so increases that at last it must be cut off by yards at a time. This some in ye University have fatally experience, & this (thow agst your will) is nigh my case. I know you are for frequent & little bills, but if you examine these you'll them of a large date, and thow often by my order after a strict scrutiny brought my Tutor, yett so long as ye payment of them been deferred as to cause them to swell to such extraordinary bulk as you now see them in.

The 3d thind I shall propose to you is ye inconvenience of a partial payment, this gives foreth opportunity's of cheating & a man that only satisfies by parcels is sure to have his goods ne'er a white ye cheaper. I might add ye grievances of being obliged to a particular man for his respective commodities, that whoever do's not pick, & choose his market never makes a good one, that whoever is forced to have his goods still of one man never grow's rich but on ye contrary
always poor: but I hope this will satisfy & work upon you so far as to acquit me & take some new method of preventing with my Tutor ye like bills for ye future, which that you may do is ye hearty desire & shall be ye utmost endeavour of
For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydall near Kendal These By ye way of London

note.value: 645. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. GEORGE FLEMING.

text.p:
I have yours of Jan. 15. 95 & I am very glad to hear yt you & your brother James are both well, which ye Lord continue: for we have a very sickly time of it in divers parts about us. Burnyates is dead, & his son will endeavour to succeed him as Carrier, in which
I wish he may have good success. Your Brother Roger came home ye week before last Xtmas, & about a week after my Cousin Swettenham came hither. He would have had Roger back again with him; but I thought he had made him a visit long enough: He is my Chaplain for ye present, & continues very orderly. Let me know, of what price, & estimation, Tanners Notitia Monastica is, you mention. Your Curate will not, I fancy, continue longer than a year, which in May next will be completed: therefore I would have you make it your main business to fit your self with many good sermons, that you may then serve your Cure, according to your Duty, & which will also be for your interest: My Lord Bishop grows very old & infirm; & if you were near him, he will, I believe, be kinder unto you than at a great Distance. Your Brothers, Dan. & Michael, are gone to Rose-Castle to make his Lordship a visit, who intend to here again shortly. The Captain intends ere long to be again for London, & so for Flanders. He hath sent away about 20 volunteers, & he hopes to march away with as many more. Your Brother Daniel hath delivered me your Account, & seven Guineas & an half Guinea, which make 11l~i - 5s - 0d which I have sent you by this Bearer - young Tho. Burnyates. There is now no sending you any silver: for all silver money here in ye Country is much worse, than it was when you were here, and ye loss your Brother Dan. hath received of yours, by
reason good silver-money is hard to be got, the more there will be to receive fer you when milled instead of this silver grows plentiful. Although I know not how Accounts stand between my Cousin Henry Brougham & me, upon my Son James his Account, having not received any Letter from him concerning ye same since I sent him 30l~i, in October last, yet I have now also sent by this young Carrier six Guineas, unto you, which make nine pounds, & which I would have you pay unto my Godson, for my Son James his use, and upon my being informed how Accounts are betwixt us, I shall ye better know what Returns to make, ye next time, by this Carrier. Your sister Alice will acquaint you what things she hath sent unto you & your brother James. My best service unto Mr Principal my Godson, & unto all ye rest of my good Friends in Oxon. The Lord bless you. I am
Just now I am told, that my Lord Bishop expects you to be at Aspatrick before Easter next.

note.value: 647. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO JAMES FLEMING.

text.p: I am very glad to discover by yours of Oct. 26. 95, and by your Brother Georges since, that you are well & continues sober & studious. Your Brother Roger came hither a little before Christmas, & behaves himself very orderly. Be a good husband of your Money Books and Cloths, & follow your studies closely, and you'll reap the honour & benefit, & I the comfort of it. Your brother George will acquaint you with what money I have sent unto your Tutor for you, & I hope you'll be sure to follow their good Advice & directions. Your brother Michael will be again for the Camp. The Lord bless you. I am

note.value: 648. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. HENRY BROUGHAM.

text.p: I wish that I had received yours before Tho. Burnyates had begun his Journey for Oxford, that I might have returned by him some more money unto you. I am glad to hear from you, that my son James his Deportment is civil, & that his Proficiency is answerable to ye Foundation you had to Build on; But herein give me leave to acquaint you, that I am much afraid you compliment both him & me: for his Accounts run so very high, that I much fear him to be otherwise than you represent him. I hope he'll have ye wit & grace to be directed by you; otherwise I am sure it will be much worse for him. If Tho. Burnyates could supply you with some more money, I will repay him upon his Return. The enclosed I hope you'll seal up & deliver unto my Son James. My service unto my ancient Friend your most worthy Provost, with my blessing unto both my Sons. I am
Sr, Your most obliged God-Father, & servant

note.value: 649. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO JAMES FLEMING.

text.p:
I have received your Letter, and one from your Tutor, wherein he acquaints me, that your Deportment is civil, & that your Proficiency, he hopes, is answerable to ye foundation you had to build upon. You
are much obliged unto him for his fair character, & you should not be wanting either to him or your self in doing cheerfully what he would have you to perform for your Honour & profit & for my satisfaction. He hath sent me your Account, which I cannot but tell you, runs much higher than I expected, & which makes me fear, that you are not so very civil, and studious, as you are Represented. Your Battles are very high, & so are divers other things in your Account, especially your Mercers & Taylors Bills. Let me know ye particulars of them, & of your Stationers Bill; & I shall then be abler to make a Judgemt of ye reasonableness of them. I thought your Sister had so ordered your Linen, as you needed not to have paid 9s - 6d for ye Altering & making thereof. You must be much more Frugal, or else there will be a great Fault; & you must be ordered by your Tutor in all things for your good, otherwise it will be much worse for you, & may be an hinderance to your Preferment. Be often adviseing with your Brother George, whiles he shall stay in Oxford, & the Lord bless you both. I am

note.value: 651. REV. HENRY BROUGHAM TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: I have been now a fortnight in ye Country for ye benefit of ye air, having been under a very bad state of health this half year. I recd your letters here, being but nine miles from Oxon; and this day I send ye key of my Study to have ye Bills you mention taken off ye file from amongst ye rest. Ire Son brought every bill himself to me at this last account: for I desired him so to do, being in hast, and having delayed ye matter to ye last.

By Civil deportment I meant no more than that his behaviour was Civil in his Station, and that he has not been guilty of those frolics
and Extravagances which his mate heretofore Sometimes led him into. By proficiency answerable &c: I thought I could not be understood to boast: because I had acquainted you, that tho~ his ffoundation was better than his Bro~'s, yet it was far from being with it ought to be. However, I said, I hoped we might make a shift to get a degree; and I am still in ye same mind: but truly I think he will by no means be fit for ye foundation; and if he do come upon it, he must expect nothing but Justice, for reasons you may possibly hear of hereafter. (I mean not any offence he has given himself).

There is so much confusion abt Guineas, that we can't tell with course to take. If Money come to any Settlement, and you have ye convenience, I could wish you would make a return; because if it please God I am able to take such a Journey, I may be in ye North before ye next return of Burn:
I am Ire Dutiful & obliged Served
At Middleton Stony near Bicester in Bucks~ To the Right Worshipful Sr Dan: ffleming at Rydal near Kendal Westmd.

note.value: 653. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Since yours by Tom, I have wrote to you twice by the Post, to neither of which have I as yet received any answer; The former was to desire you to assist me with some more money, which I hope you will not refuse, now at this juncture especially, when I have lost so much by that Little I had sent; for Guineas are here (& at London not so much) but at 24s, or 25s, or at most 26. The other letter was to know whether James should now enter upon the Foundation or no; his Tutors opinion is that he is not fit for it. The news here is about the non Subscribing members some of which are; The Burgesses for Apulby, all ye Kts. & Burgesses for Warwickshire, except Tho.
Grey Esq~. For Oxfordshire, ye Lt. Norreys, Sr Rob. Jenkinson, Heneage Finch, Sr Adieu. Norreys, Mr Rowney, James Bertie, Sr Rob. Dashwood. Sr Adieu. Seymour for Totnes in Dev. ye 2 Kts. for Dorsetsh. & also for Somersetsh. Sr John Leveson Gower for
Newcastle under Lyne; ye Burgasses for ye town of Salop. & several others. Mr Tenors Book Sr you writ about, is only an account of the Founders of ye Religious Houses, without any remarks upon their lives, together with the time when, & the place where. The Papists of this County are now most of them brought here to Oxford, and the Train-Bands have received orders to be ready upon the least notice. Sr I have sent you by this Bearer an Oxford Almanac, & so desiring your Blessing, rest
Sr Your most obedient son to command

Sr Charles Carterett one of ye members of ye H. of Com~ons who had refused to sign the Association, desired leave to sign the same upon Tuesday, saying he had better considered of it; & begged ye pardon of ye House for his refusal & he signed ye same accordingly, as all the rest have time allowed them to do, by order of ye House till ye 10th of this month. Barnard Howard is com~itted to ye Tower, Sr
Roger L'Estrange to Newgate, & Coll. Harris & Mr Edmd. Elliat to ye Gate House. A warrant being given out against ye E. of Iran son to Dk. Hamilton he hath surrendered himself & is under a guard at his own house. on ye 2d were taken up Lt Brudenell, Lt Ross of Ireland, Mr Hen. Burleigh, one Clifford who was a Brigadier formerly, & sent to the Tower. my Lt Peterborough being indisposed is under
confinement at his own house, & so is Sr Hen. Sheres, Sr Rich Hart one of ye members for Bristol in ye last Parl. is com~itted to ye Gate house, & Sr John Friend is in ye Custody of a Messenger wh many others.

A Messenger who was sent down to search Sr Will. Perkins house found a great quantity of arms in an Outhouse buried under ground. some of this Sr may be news, & I had it from a Letter writ by one of ye under Secret. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal These.

note.value: 656. REV. HENRY FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Being two nights last week at Rose to wait on the Bishop, and he and his Lady requiring me give you their Service, I thought it my
duty both in relation to you and them by the first opportunity to doe it after this manner. I have received a Letter from Brother James of the 19th instant; wherein he says that a relation of Ours & Cus. Wilson's, as he says, tho~ we have not seen him, was last week seized and presently committed to Ridding Goal, as one concerned in the Plot. He was taken under the name of Birkett a Kendalian, which he utterly dinys; but the name he gives out is William Herbert Collingwood . Last Thursday the Corporation of Appleby did unanimously sign the Association verbatim as it is in the Votes, and next day sent it by the Post to Sr John Louder to present it to the King. The Bishop has likewise drawn a short Address with the Association (differing in nothing from that of the House of Com~ons, but in the word Revenge , which is left out and the sense otherwise expressed) which is to be
carried through the Diocese by the Arch-Deacon and Chancellor, and this Deanoray hath orders to meet next Friday at Appleby for that End. Sr I beg your pardon for this trouble, and leave to remain.
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal-hall These.

note.value: 661. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. GEORGE FLEMING.

text.p:
I am very sorry to hear, that you have had so dangerous a Fit of Sickness; and it is well that you are in good health again. Make much of ye Living you have, for God knows whether I shall live, & be able, to help you to a better. I have ordered John Harrison of Kendal (one of my Wool-Buyers, & now at London) to return Twenty Pounds unto you, so soon as he can, for ye use of your
self and your Brother James. I intend shortly to send your Brother Daniel unto Aspatrick to serve you there as well as he can. Tell your Brother James, that I have seen a Letter of his unto my Son Henry, with which I am not well pleased, and that I have received James his Letter, wherein he only writes for money, & acquaints me with Mr Saul his Death. I was in hopes, to have heard from him of his Resolving to follow his Study closely, & of his using his utmost endeavours to get to be chosen a Poor child, as I writ formerly unto you. I hear there hath been lately an Election in Queens, but neither you nor he hath acquainted me therewith. If any of James juniors hath been elected, I shall be sorry for it, and I would know how many of ye Batlers are his Seniors, & who they are. I like not his being so long without a Tutor; and in case you and He cannot pitch upon one, then pray acquaint Mr Provost that I desire him to appoint one for my son James. I do not well understand ye Figures in ye Pedigree you sent me, as xx 13. &c. My grandson Edward Wilson dyed ye last week, & was buried upon Thursday last. The Lord fit us all for our Deaths. Let James see this Letter, I intending it to serve you both. Let me know ye date of my Letter wherein ye Promise is you mention; and then I shall give you an Answer. Old Mr Saul first heard of his Sons Death from James his Letter unto me. Your Brother James concludes his Letter unto me thus. - This I desire you to take notice of & shall expect your return. - Acquaint him, that when I was at Oxford, Sons used not thus bluntly to compliment their Fathers. The Lord bless you both. I am

note.value: 663. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I have received a letter from you of, 26 Apr. & another since. In the former you are pleased to mention an order you had given John Harrison, to return us 20£, I have his bill, but ye money is not payable till ye 24th and ye party that's to pay't, being not in town until then, I can give you no further account of it. It's true there there hath been an election in Q. Coll. but it was of Fellows whose names, if I did not give you, it was because I supposed James to have done it; (there names are Teasdale, Simpson, Gibson, & Huchinson) but
as for Poor-Children, it has not been yet, nor will as far as I can hear till about Act or Midsum~er. Mr Waugh is James's Tutor, & when I spoke to him, he was extremely pleased you had made choice of him; I shall be glad to know with whom James's money is to be entrusted. I am sorry, Sr, to hear by your last letter yt my Brother Daniel (to whom I shall always be ready to make my acknowledgments) hath been put to so much trouble on my behalf at Aspatrick, but I hope now he'll be able by your assistance, so to manage things there, as I shall not be obliged, to put so long a stop to my studies, as a Northcountry journey will cause. You cannot but be sensible, Sr, how great a task ye Sac. Function is: it's reckoned great impudence to pretend to be Marster in a science in which a man's not well instructed; & if so: Alas! what's ye condition of such, as to go live upon a Cure for which they are not duly qualified. The Learned Mr Dodwell does not as yet think himself fit for ye Holy-function, Alas then how am I. I do not write this, Sr, out of any dislike eather to ye Pace or Function, (for I protest if I could but believe myself capable of performing ye duty required, I should have saved both my self & you ye trouble of this Letter) but when in conscience I think myself to do yt better by another then by my self, I hope, none will be so hard upon me, as to use compulsion, an Argument as yet, never thought to have ye least relish of Xtianity, whereupon I cannot doubt of your consent to, & assistance in my being at Oxford, which I shall employ to ye best advantage & so desiring your blessing
rest Sr Your most obedt. Son.

The Pedigree Sr is as I find it in ye Ms. I have seen Dugds.
Ms of Kts. & also Vincents Ms of ye same & Anth. Woods Ms corrections of Dugd. Bar. the most material part of which you shall have a Copy of. Mr Kennet hath now Published his Antiquities of Ambrosden in 4o. Mr Gibson is now this week gone to London to take care of ye Arch Deacons
Book which is there now ready for the Press. For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydall near Kendal in Westmorland These

note.value: 667. REV. HENRY FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
This comes to waite on you upon a double account, both to acquaint you with my intention of going shortly to Oxford, and to request your assistance in my business there. You were first pleased to send me thither, and engage me in taking of Degrees, therefore I hope you'll now be pleased to help me in taking the two last, namely Bachelor and Doctor in Divinity. It will be a chargeable undertaking, Yet much cheaper this year than another there being no public Act and the assurance I have of company to contribute in part. I may save near 20l~i in leaving Queens College, (as I am desired
to doe by a Gentleman that takes his Degrees with me) but I am loath to disgust the Provost and Fellows there, lest it prove injurious to my Brother James if he designs for the foundation: Yet I shall be constrained to do it Unless you please to supply me with some Money, it being so scarce and difficult to get up that I cannot possibly procure enough without borrowing, which I am unwilling to doe. It's not often that I make requests to you of this nature or indeed of any, and therefore I hope to succeed. I think to be at Rydal tomorrow fortnight or in a few days after in my road, to receive Your com~ands, and in the mean time Pray give me leave to rely on Your favour, and remain
My Brother William came hither last night and I think designs for Louder tomorrow and for Rydal some time next week. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydale These.

note.value: 669. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. JOHN WAUGH.

text.p:
I thank you for ye Favour of yours, which came but lately unto my hand. When my Letters are directed unto me at Rydal, Westmerland, then they come by ye Yorkshire Post, & are longer coming hither; But when they are directed unto me at Rydal near Kendal, then they come much sooner by ye Lancashire Post. I am glad to hear, that you find my son James willing and tractable, hoping by your good Advice he may daily improve in knowledge & virtue. For his use, I have sent you ten Guinneas, as ye most payable money I can send you by this Bearer. When as my Cousin Henry Brougham's Account is settled, & I know what, & to whom to pay, I will take
care to discharge my part. My humble service to Mr Provost, & all other my kind Friends in Queens. I am
Shall we not hope for some things of ye Late Bishop of Lincoln to be published.

note.value: 670. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. GEORGE FLEMING.

text.p:
I have writ unto my Lord Bishop, & I have sent your brother Daniel unto Rose & Aspatrick, who will acquaint you with what he hath done. My Lord is willing that you shall continue at Oxford longer, so as you study Divinity, & fit yourself for ye serving of your cure in person, according to your Duty. Your curate is so ill to deal with, as he hath quite tyred your Brother Dan. He could not get so much payable money there as to pay Mr Overend. I have sent you ten Guineas by this Bearer for your self, & so much by him for Mr Waugh for ye use of James. You'll scarcely believe how difficult it is to Receive or Pay money, that will pass. Yours of ye 5th. instant I have, & I am troubled yt your 20l~i Bill should be so ill answered. I think you had best keep ye Bill until you shall receive 20l~i of good & payable money. I have ordered your Brother Daniel to write unto Mr Harrison my wool-man; who I hope will take such course with his correspondent at London, as that you shall be well answered. I have lately received a Letter from Mr Waugh, & I have writ unto him by this Bearer. For ye rest I referr you to my last
Letter. Give my best service unto your most obliging Principal, & unto all other my good Friends. Be often adviseing & directing of your brother James. My son Will. is now here, & I have not heard from Michael since his leaving of London. The Lord bless you all. I am

note.value: 671. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO JAMES FLEMING.

text.p: I am very glad, that Mr Waugh, your Tutor, hath given you so good a character; and I hope you'll continue to make it good, by your prudence, civility, & hard studying. If you shall be so unfortunate as to neglect ye present time, you'll be sure hereafter to repent it, when it will be too late: therefore be sure to employ your precious time, as becomes a prudent & Religious man, & be not guilty of Idleing, triffleing, or Folly. Your Tutor & Brother will acquaint you with what I have sent for you. Be advisable for your Honour & Welfare; and ye Lord bless you & preserve you out of all ill company. I am

note.value: 674. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Yours of June ye 23 I received, not long after my Bros arrival
here, who had ye honour of a Dr grand compounder degree. Last week great expectation was here at ye Assizes to know what sentence would be passed of a Townsman, who killed a Scholar with a bottle; The Company differed so much in their Relation, ye Jury brought him in only guilty of Mans-Slaughter, and ye Judge com~and'd him not to keep Ale for ye future; And no less at Winser with most of our Gentry to see ye Duke of Gloster installd. We cannot tell when to expect either admittance for ye jur Fellows or an election for poor children, which was never known to be deferd so long; Whether ye Library building occasions it or no, I cannot imagine. Which that I
may answer your last, is ye hearty desire & shall be ye utmost endeavour of
For Sr Daniel Fleming att Rydal These.

note.value: 675. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I received yours by the Post, but Tom is not able to answer ye contents of it; wherefore I desire some other expedient may be found out. The guineas you sent me at Lent for James's use, were 2 of them laid out in exercise in ye Schools, Pocket mony's, & some other small things; the 3d was paid according to my Cousin Browhams order, & ye other three have I given Mr Waugh. James's accounts are so intricate yt we cannot do any thing with them, unless we have your assistance. For by your letters to me I am of opinion he's indebted to you about 15£ when as they make it ye contrary, for I cannot see any account given of what you sent in October. last, nor any
receipt of it; I suppose it was 30£; If you sent nothing then by Tom ye accounts may be right. Sr I have sent you what collections I have about ye Flamings; & Mr Lhwyd's proposals, he hath a great many Benefactors amongst which Dr Mills is one; Dr Dixon gives his service to you. Mr Provost was not so kind to my brother, ye Dr, as might be expected, but I suppose there was no love lost. so desiring your blessing I rest
The election of poor-Children is not yet over. July 28.

Tom gave me this morning two guineas which I desire you Sr to repay, & hope you'll be pleased to find some way of assisting me
further, for here's no ticking, scarce for two pence, without being put in mind of it, monies are here so scarce. For Sr Daniel Fleming These.

note.value: 678. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. JOHN WAUGH.

text.p:
I have Received (by Tho. Burnyates) yours of ye 28th of ye last month, & upon ye perusal of ye Account I find no difference, save that ye 30li sent by Burnyates unto my Cousin Brougham was not in July
95, but rather in October following. I was owing him, I believe, 19l~i - 16s - 00d according to his Account of Fibre. 1 95/6. Since which time (Feb. 6. 95) I sent to my Son Goo. F. six Guineas (then 9l~i) to be paid by him unto my Cousin Hen. Brougham, for my son James F. his use. In April following I returned by Jo. Harrison of Kendal unto my Son Goo. F. 20l~i viz. one half for himself, & ye other half thereof for my son James F: and in June last sent you 11l~i which you mention in your Letter, as also 3l~i - 6s - 0d received from my son Goo. F. If herein I be mistaken, it shall be rectified, & what shall appear due from me upon stateing of ye Account, shall be answered. I doubt not but yt you & my Son Goo. F. will so adjust this affair, as that right may be done to all parties; I thank you for your care of my son James, & I hope you'll give my service to my Ancient Friend Mr Provost, & to my other Acquaintance with you. I am,
Sr Your obliged Friend to serve you

note.value: 682. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: I delayed to answer yours of ye 13 of Aug. in hopes to give you at ye same time a good account of ye Election of P. Children at Queens, but that not proceeding according to our desires, it may be very proper to give you the account of ye plain matter of fact, which is this.

Upon Wednesday night last James came to my chamber, to acquaint me that orders were given to each of ye Battlers in particular, that expected to be elected poor Child~, to provide an Epistle for the Provost, according to custom; amongst these, though Senior, he had no notice, & so consequently not to stand; upon this he knew not what to do, but as I advised him provided his Epistle, & ye next morning gave his Tutor it to correct as the other did theirs; but his Tutor keeping ye Epistle, we heard no more of it till ye Election was over, which was upon Friday last. Yesterday Mr Waugh came to my Chamber & expressed a great concern for what had happened, & said yt Mr Browham had informed them James was not designed for ye
foundation; but as soon as he had received James's Epistle he went directly to ye Provost, but received no other answer then this, that he had pitched upon his men, tho nothing was then done, & no election till ye next day.

If I might, Sr, advise upon the matter, I am of opinion yt its ye best to remove him from thence and that for these reasons. For 1st that what restraint the Foundation laid upon him is now taken off, whereby there's a very great temptation to idleness, if nothing else, those in his circumstances being not thought worth the taking notice of. Again whatever his expenses might be before this, daily experience teaches us, yt after the thoughts of a Foundation are given over these constantly increase; and it cannot be very eligible to buy a little, a very little learning (if we may compute by the progress he hath as yet made) at the expense of money's, & corruption of morals. If he were under Dr Mill's care I do not question but we should be able to give you a much better account of him, & cure him of such things as cannot be expeted there where ye best are culpable. I should be very willing to spend some time this winter upon him, & set him in so true a light both of things here, & at Rydall, as may make him afterwards fit to judge for himself; but you know best, Sr, what to do.

I hope, Sr, you'll please to excuse my forgetting to mention ye 10 Guineas you were pleased to send me by Tom ye last time, & I desire you will do ye same this time, which and what I received from
your Woolman will I hope serve this winter. I hope Sr you received a letter of mine by ye Post, in which I desired to keep ye sum~ returned me by a bill from Leeds, which you not contradicting my necessities obliged me to make use off. I shall always, Sr, make it my business, as I am very sensible it is my interest & duty, to be as grateful as its possible; In ye Spring I shall be desirous to leave this place if you please, & and in the interim I desire your blessing & the tender of my service to all my brothers & sisters & rest
Sr Your most obliged obedient Son
Sr the Little you mentioned in you last letter is of no moment, & I shall give you if you please a full account of it when I see you.
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal These.

note.value: 684. JAMES FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
After what manner to give you account of my late disappointment, least you should impulit it to my neglicence, and disrespect for ye Foundation, I hope you are satisfied; To co~ply with your proposals & in persuance to your orders, I provided my Epistle at ye election, thow all to no purpose, for Mr Prove was pleased to admit 5 of my jurs which was not known before; I might signify to you ye great encouragement I have for removing to Edmond-Hall (and ye small
inducement to tarry) since ye loss of this, which may be supplied by my Bros instructions & example. This morning my Bro: was very well. My duty to you and love to all Bro: & Sisters, I am
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal By way of London

note.value: 686. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. JOHN WAUGH.

text.p:
Yours, & my Son's Letters coming lately unto my hand, I was much surprised at my Son James his being past by at your late Election. Whatsoever may be pretended, I always designed him for ye Foundation, in case my Countrymen would think fit so far to favour him. It is true, that my Cousin Henry Brougham wrote to me Feb. 26 95/96 & endeavoured to dissuade me from his standing to be a Poor Child, adding these words, And if he come upon it, he must expect nothing but Justice, for Reasons you may possibly hear of hereafter, I mean not any Offence he has given himself . My Cousin dying soon after these Lines came to my hand, I had not ye opportunity of having them explained by himself nor have I yet heard from any others what these Reasons should be. To condemn my son without an Hearing, or me without notice of any pretended Offence, is something extraordinary, & is what one could not reasonably expect from an Ancient Friend or Acquaintance, much less from
so knowing a Body, Least my Son should be too much discouraged, I have writ to my son George to take care of his Brother, hoping that you'll advise him therein for ye best. As concerning my Cousin Brougham's Papers, inscribed Not Entered or Omitted , if I had a copy of them, I should then acquaint you with my thoughts of them. Let me know by this Bearer what is due from my Son, & to whom, that care may be taken for the discharge thereof. I am much obliged unto you, & all others who have showed or shall show any kindness unto any of my Sons, or unto my self, & I shall remain

note.value: 687. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I have received yours by Tom. & consulted Mr Principal & Mr Waugh, who both conclude that to remove James is the only way left to do him any good. Mr Principal is very willing to admit him upon the conditions you mention, yt he'll be sober, civil, a good husband & governable , & will enter him how you please, but I am of opinion that we can never do any thing with him a Batteler, who is allowed to Battle no more than a Poor-Child of Queens, at which rate I have heard him say he could not, not to say, would not live, so yt we should be the more troubled with him, by how much the hall is stricter than Queens; & besides all our Battelers here, are such as afterwards are made servitors when a place is vacant. If a Com~oner,
the charge will be but little more, and yt is in Battles; but yet cannot Battle nigh so much as he does now at Q. & I shall take care, whilst here, to keep him within bounds; or acquaint you with it. The V. Principal is all the Tutor in the Hall except (Mr Principal) & for me to be Tutor too James would be a breach betwixt us, and for so small a time as I shall be here, Sr, will not be worth it. I say not this, Sr, to avoid any trouble, but I know his condition requiers more then one to take care of him: Mr V. P. may instruct him in Philosophy which he wants, & I shall spend the nights with him in Gram~er & ye Classics of which he knows little, & shall make him study the day's by me, so that if you receive not a good account of him it shall evidently his own fault.

Sr without some monies to Mr Waugh we cannot well proceed, for James owes above 12£ to the Coll. for battles, which were before the death of my Cos. Browham, and should be paid before James leave ye Coll. I wish Sr you could return him 15£ for so much he wants for ye Coll. & some other expenses, which he (Mr Waugh) says, Sr, you have owned to be due to Mr Browham. Mr Waugh gives his service to you; & has explained yt part of Mr Browhams Letter, which was in yours, by which he makes ye Provost, however he excuses him, the more unkind to James. Mr Browhams Letter understands by not by his own fault or such words, yt it was by the fault of my B. H. if, Sr, you think it worth ye hearing, my next shall be more clear or rather when I come to Rydal; I desire Sr to hear as soon from you as you can, & so desiring your blessing rest

Sr I have not yet seen Tom
but received your Letter from James, & to save ye Post writ thus, not time to look it over. For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rudal near Kendal These

note.value: 688. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. GEORGE FLEMING.

text.p:
I have yours of ye 14th instant; and I am much obliged unto Mr Principal, that he will be pleased to admit my son James upon ye conditions of his assuring Dr Mill, ye Vice Principal, & yourself to be sober, civil, studious, a good Husband & Governable; and if he will not do this, & perform it, I wish I had him at home, rather than he should give you all so much trouble, & be so great a charge to me, I fear, to Little, or no purpose. I am yet so in ye Dark concerning James & his Affairs, as I know not well what to direct in that matter. If you could buy him a small priced Horse, & send him hither by Tho. Burnyates, a visit here probably might do him good, & I shall then know ye better what to do. But if that be not approved of, then do with him as Mr Principal, Mr Waugh & you shall think best. You are upon ye place & may judge better of this than I can do at a distance. As to his being a com~oner, it will make higher and increase my charge, & will I fear a little improve him; but this also I referr unto you (in case he shall not come hither) & ye naming of his Tutor. You take no notice of your Receiving of ye Twenty Guineas I last sent (you & James) by Tho. Burnyates.
Let Mr Waugh have as much thereof as you can, & what shall remain due to him, & ye Executor or Administrator of my Cousin Hen. B. I will take care to send by Burnyates at his next being for Oxford, (or sooner, in case I can meet with a convenient return) if in ye mean time I may have an Account of ye particulars. Let your Brother James peruse this Letter, & let him consider what Trouble (to say no more) he gives us all. My best service to your worthy Principal, & to Mr Waugh; & ye Lord bless you & James. I am

note.value: 697. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I beg your pardon for no sooner wishing you a happy new year, & hope ye Country air has so cleared James's eyes as yt for ye future he'll be able easily to see his own interest, & as readily embrace it. I desire you would be pleased when you shall think fit to return him hither, to qualify him to pay off all former scores, yt there may not be the least temptation to follow the old track. I have had several Dun~s upon his account, & Mr Waugh hath not wanted his share, but ye most importunate is Mr Browham, but of this Mr Waugh has given you account, yet has omitted in his own account, Tutorage. Supposing James, Sr, come up with ye Carrier, it will be much all one in respect of charge, how he's entered; For if he be Bachl in ye Vnivty Michas next then will he be Bachl in the Hall the Act before, so yt
he'll be an Vndergraduate & subject to a Tutor but just a Quarter. What monies, Sr, you send for his use (which I wish may be betwixt 15 & 20 Pounds) I shall most willingly take the charge of, & also of him if you please as Mr Prinl is now desirous I should, & shall endeavour to give you as good, or at ye worst as exact an account of both as I can.

As for my self, Sr, I am wholly at your disposal, & shall either come down, or tarry here as you shall please to direct, & should be much more desirous of the former, had I not too to prevailing an Argumt for the latter. For having made use of a leaning or stooping posture when I writ or read in my study, found my self most of ye last Summer & all this Winter troubled by times with most violent pains in my Breast, but not in ye least imagining the reason, was so far from omitting ye cause, yt it rather seemed to be the only ease I had; & might have so continued, till ye discovery had been of no use, if Mr Principal had not one day observed my coat look very fresh all over excepting ye Breast where it was thread bare & so cautioned me against leaning. But besides this pain in my Breast, I alway's seem to have something sticking in my throat, which always when I read, & sometimes when I swallow is like to stifle me, & whenever of late I have attempted to do ye duty in ye Chapl have not been able to go through ye service, but forced to cut short or leave imperfect. Some call it a convultion, others give it harder names, but me ye hopes of being cleared of it this spring; which makes me desirous to tarry till capable (If I may be so happy) of doing my duty in ye Country. The fears, Sr, of not being able to shake of this infirmity, & ye thoughts of with charge & trouble I have all along & daily do put you too, are not a little damp upon my spirits, & make me one time desire to be with you, & another to try 1st what Physic can do for me; so being least able to advice for my self, as at all times, so now in particular am desirous to know your pleasure, having had frequent proof yt as you know, so you advice ye best, what's most convenient for
Sr Your most obliged & obedt Son
I desire you'll write to Mr Principal, & yt my sister send me some shirts.

I desire, Sr, whether I come down or no Mr Overend may be kept at Aspatrick; & if it be your pleasure I leave Oxon~ now, hope you'll let me know it as soon as you can, & yt you'll be pleased to assist me Pith 30£ to capacitate me to leave ye place as I have lived in it with credit. But if you think fit to continue me here, yt may perhaps be of ye least, but I will not think of trespassing higher.
We are so in love with our Plate here, yt the old Dons make what interest I believe they can to be excused parting with it. Dr Barnerd Fellow formerly of St Johs Coll. died yesterday.
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydall near Kendall These

note.value: 698. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. JOHN WAUGH.

text.p: Yours (sans Date) by my Son James Fleming, and your Letter of ye 11th instant by ye Post, are come unto my hand; and you should have heard from me ere this, had I known who had been my Cousin Henry Brougham's Administrator. I have returned money (notwithstanding our present confusion about money in this Country) unto my son George, for ye paying off what is due unto you from my son James; & George will, I doubt not, upon his Receiving thereof, satisfy you, & other lawful claimers, wherein I hope you'll assist him. There is due to my two sons, Roger & James, five pounds for their Caution-money; which I hope will be allowed in their Accounts. I have ordered a Copy of my Cousin Hen. Brougham's Account to be written, which my son George will com~unicate unto you, hoping that will give full satisfaction, & will prevent ye demanding of more than is right. In case my Cousin Jo. Brougham be his Brothers Administrator, I doubt not but all things will therein be fairly transacted, and so I hope if you be concerned therein. I thank you for all your kindnesses, & I shall ever remain
Sr Your affectionate and obliged Friend & Servant

note.value: 703. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO BISHOP SMITH OF CARLISLE.

text.p: I writ lately to my Son George at Oxford, concerning his coming into the country, wherein I acquainted him, that I believed your Lordship & ye Parish did expect his being at Aspatrick shortly, & that I did ye same. The last Post hath brought me a Letter from Doctor Mill, my sons very kind Friend to which I know not what to answer until your Lordship shall be pleased to favour me with your Advice therein. Having lately congratulated Sr Joseph Williamson (my very good Friend) upon his being sworn one of His Majesties Privy Council in England, he was pleased to make me a very kind Return, wherein your Lordship being mentioned, I have herein sent you his Letter, as also that from Doctor Mill, that your Lordship may have them both read unto you. True Friends growing fewer, I most value their kindness, therefore pray return me the Letters enclosed by this Bearer. I am very glad to hear, by my sons Henry and James, of your Lordships good Health, & so of your Ladies. I shall heartily wish you both many happy New Years, & I shall ever remain,
My Lord, Your Lordships most obedient & most obliged Servant
All here are your most humble servants. For ye Bishop of Carlisle.

note.value: 704. BISHOP SMITH OF CARLISLE TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: I have yors by the bearer, and do return you my thanks for it & for your sending me the enclosed from Dr Mill, which I have had read over to me with very great satisfaction, being extremely pleased, as I doubt not you are, with that very good character He therein gives of your Son George: I was always willing He might have time to complete his studies at Oxford; and upon ye Accts which ye Dr gives I shall much more readily agree to what's requested now if you will please to do so too; hoping that by Mich~s we may see Him (as is promised) to all our satisfacc~ons. I must thank you also for favouring me with a Sight of the L~re~ you recd from our good friend Sr Joseph Williamson, whom I think, you did well to congratulate &c. I also did the like; and I perceive He takes it very kindly from us both. I have herein, as you desire, returned both the L~re~s, which I hope will come safe to your hand again & I question not will be so kept by you, as they deserve.
Mine and my wife's best Respects & Services to your self & all yors in Ridale is all I have to add at prsent but that I am ever
Worthy Sr Your very faithful Servant
ffor my worthy ffriend Sr Daniel ffleming Knight, These at Ridale

note.value: 705. DR. HENRY FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
The greatest news I meet withal in this Town is a List of the
Com~issioners for the Cappitation Act; who are these viz. Mr Ed. Wilson, Mr Tho. Hebblethwaite, Mr Chambre, Mr Tho. Godsalve, Mr Bird, Mr Winder, Mr Reg. Dobson, Mr Rich. Baynes, and Mr. And.
Hudleston R. General. Cousin Preston was brought to Lancaster last night and was to be buried this Day: Its said Sr Wilfrid Lawson lays claim to part of his Estate. I have just now received a Letter from Mr Matthew Rut Schoolmaster of Ravenstondale to beg your favour in the Election for a Master at Blencow, Mr Ogle being shortly to leave that place. He has a very good character now for his learning and diligence, and may probably doe very well upon a removal: He has given Tho. Dawson another Feoffee's interest. I am

note.value: 708. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: John Harrison Bill of Thirty Pounds has been paid me very punctually; & I have paid off Mr Waugh and Mr Browham, as the acquits. show; if Mr Browhams acquit. be not as it ought to be, as Mr Waugh & I scarce believe it is, we desire directions how to write a letter. Those 2 acqts., deducting five pounds caution, show what remains in my hands; and I desire your directions what to do with ye Bills now in my hands unpay'd, which Mr Browham had nothing to do with.

That you have been pleased, Sr, upon Mr Principals request, to continue me here until Michaelmas, was what I had given over to expect, & so can esteem no less than a singular favour conferred upon me; & therefore if I come short of your expectations, it must not be thought Mr Principals, & I hope shall not be my fault; but I know no further about his letter than that he had wrote to you. I have received Sr the Fifteen Guineas you sent by Tom. & must alway's acknowledge the great charges you have been at upon my account, yet cannot think yt you'll leave me now at ye last push, which make me desire another Bill of you of 10£ by the same hands, to be paid me by Mr Dyson who pd~ ye last when he comes again to Oxford which will be within this Six weeks; & be pleased to let me repay it you when I shall be in ye country, if Aspatria cannot do it sooner. I wish might have also
something to pay of Rog. & James's ticks here, 5 pounds might perhaps do so. So Sr desiring your blessing I rest
Sr your most obed~. son to com~d

Sr I give you my most hearty thanks for the Charr-Pot you was pleased to send me, & have disposed of it as directed; Mr Principal and Mr Waugh give their serve to you. Sr I have sent you an Almanac. We have nothing new now but Mr Tyrrels I. Vol. of his Angle. History which comes to ye Conquest, and is fallen into ye hands of ye Critics who spare not to lay open all its faults.
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal. with a Book.

note.value: 712. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
I should sooner have answered your last letter had I not been
desirous at ye same time to give you an account of the receipt of ye Bill you pleased to mention in it; but that being not yet come to my hands makes me now give over all hopes of meeting with it. I am sorry you were not then, but I hope since resolved of sending James up this Act, unless you think fit to bestow him some other way, then you have formerly designed. For not to insist upon his Degree which requires his attendance here, my being now upon the place to have an eye constantly upon him, may possibly be an opportunity not again to be had, & such as may have (after this his being in ye Country) better effects upon him then any other method can be found out. I hope, Sr, you'll be pleased to excuse this my freedom it proceeding from no other then the desire I have to see James do well & if it should fall out otherwise it might not be in his power to blame any other then himself for it. Idleness, Sr, you know has never been though productive of any thing good, but on ye contrary ever pernicious to youth; this consideration, Sr, moves me to be the more earnest in soliciting his return, that he may be employed, & as he has upon your account many willing to oblige him, so he may be in a capacity to receive their favours. Once more give me leave to desire his company, yt it may not be said, yt when he was desirous to remove to a place of better instruction & example, you wear not pleased to consent unto it. What's due here in town from my Brothers seems all very clear except ye Chandlers Bill which Mr Waugh & I'll examine if you'll please to send money by Tom, & send you ye Bills & acquittances.

Now after my request for my Brother, be pleased Sr to receive one for my self. What you pleased to order me by Bill, not coming to me makes my necessities the greater, living now upon credit. I must therefore desire you to supply me with what you shall please to think fitting for me, to clear 2 Quarters Battles, my Hebrew Tutor, & Bottanick Professor with both which I shall have concluded in a month or 2, add to these a new suite of clothes & other necessary expenses,
to defray all these charges, Sr, will I fear require Twenty Pounds at ye least; this I hope is the last quarter I am to tarry here, & you have been all along so extraordinary kind to me, yt I cannot doubt you'll suffer me to want in this.
Mr Waugh has found by my Cos. Browham's Books that Roger & James' Caution was charged to you, but James's never paid to the Bosser, so that my Cos. Browham stands charged with it.

Mr Kennet's Book of ye Aniqties of Ambrosden was above my hands to purchase, being a 4o of 14 or 15 shillings price. If you please, Sr, to give orders how you'll have it bound, I shall take care of it. Mr. Terrils Book is in Folo price 20 shillings. Mr Principal is of opinion its well worth your having for as much as ye Author he supposes ye best versed in Engl~. History of any man in the Kingdom. Mr Principle never read the Book. Mr Tanner is very cautious, but told me yt he supposed it would not answer your expectation, & that its doubted by many whether he'll proceed or no any further; its true the Bookseller, after abut half of ye Book was printed off would proceed no further so yt the Author was putt to ye inconvenience of both the Charge of Printing & trouble of compiling ye work. Those who dislike the Book think he does not account right for ye Original of Govmt which is not the least part of this vol. None I meet with but grant it to contain several good things, nor any undertake to vindicate it from a great many faults. So Sr Desiring your Blessing rest
Sr Your most obed~t Son to com~and
For Sr Daniel Fleming at Rydal near Kendal These

note.value: 718. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: I received yours of ye 6th together with my Brother Daniels ye last night, & being desirous to give you ye news of this place by ye 1st Post, went directly to enquire for Dyson ye Carrier but found he was not as in come to Oxford. Mr Teasdel one of ye Fellows of Qc Coll: came to town a few days ago not to say weeks (after amost a years being in ye North, & a little at London) & died yesterday in ye afternoon of a Fever. Mr Dale another of ye Fellows is under ye same distemper, & by ye generality given for lost. The former is much lamented by all yt knew him, & this will be by ye admirers of good Discipline to whom Qc was indebted for what it had. These, Sr, had nothing extrordinary in their distemper, but being upon this melancholy subject, I cannot pass by ye death of Mr Harding which had something singurlar in it; he was one of ye senior Fell. of Trin. Coll. Bach. of Divty a Great Tutor & of the 1st rank for Learning, & little inferior in years; this Gent having been too free with a Doctor of Physs reputation of his own Coll. was putt in ye Vice Chanl Court for it, & finding himself in danger of Beggin Pardon was so enraged at it, yt a sickness of 2 or 3 day's put a period to his life. he refused to see ye Gent whom he had wronged, & so became lamented of none but censer'd by most, So, Sr, begging your blessing I rest
Sr Your most obedient son to command

Sr fearing to miss ye Post, I shall answer ye rest of
your letter when I have seen Dyson. I desire you would please to consider how I may send my Books ye Best & Cheapest. For Sr Daniel Fleming These.

note.value: 722. SIR DANIEL FLEMING TO REV. GEORGE FLEMING.

text.p:
I have Received your Letters of Aug. 13 & of Sept. 1. 97; & I am glad to hear that you are well, & that you have Received ye 14l~i from Dyson. The best & cheapest way, I think, to send all your & your Brothers Books & other things hither will be to send them by your Oxford waggon unto London (in Dale-Boxes, or rather made up in a Pack) with this Direction viz. For Mr Thomas Brathwait at Kendal, to be left with Mr John Gowling at the Castle-Inn in Wood-street, London, to be sent by Kendal-Carrier. Do not mention your own name in ye Directions: for then they will come hither, as Merchants Goods, much cheaper. Thomas Brathwait aforesaid hopes to be at London about ye end of the next week, where he intends to stay about a Fourthnight; and if you can get all ye things sent unto London in that time, he will take care of them, pay for their Carriage, & send them hither; otherwise he will speak to Mr Jo. Gowling to do it for him. I hear Tho. Burnyate will begin his Journey for Oxford ye last of this month, by whom I shall write further, & send you more money. As concerning ye Discharging of your Brothers old Ticks, I must refer you to my Letter of ye First of July last. I like Mr Kennets Parochial Antiquities so well, as I should be glad to hear
of his Publishing his second Part, & of his improving ye History of ye Baronage of England, or ye Monasticon Anglicanum. My best service to your most Learned & obliging Principal. Enquire what Mr Tanner is doing. The Lord bless you.
My Cousin Will Kirkby of Ashslack is lately dead. If you are ye waggoners servant, he'll be more careful of your Goods.
Direct your Goods unto Mr Thomas Brathwait at Kendal to be left with Mr John Gowling at ye Castle-Inn in Wood-street London to be sent by Kendal-Carrier.

note.value: 727. REV. GEORGE FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: I have received your kind Letters, & the Thirty Pounds by Tom. I should not have been thus long in Oxon~, but yt I am unwilling to be without Company in so long a journey. I hope my Boxes are now with you, I could wish, without any injury from ye waters; but for fear of ye worst, I desire they may be put in a dry place, such as is yt over ye Brew-house; or the Books taken out of ye Boxes. I desire yt such books as are wet may not be brought nigh ye fire, or opened. The Box in which my Stud. Gown is I desire may be nailed up again if you chare to open it, for its full of papers I would not willingly have seen. The Boxes are in number 7 & one of them James's. his Stud. Gown is in it. A Letter, Sr, from one of my Brothers giving an account of what Quarter my Boxes have had, & meeting me at Park-House or Ingleton, would be very acceptable, for I am very uneasy till I hear what case my Books are in. So Sr desiring your blessing, rest
Your most oblig~d and obedt Son to Com~and

note.value: 731. BISHOP SMITH OF CARLISLE TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
This last week I recd your kind L~re dated ye 8th Instant, and was very glad to hear of your & your ffamily's good Health, which I shall ever wish the continuance of. Your son George is now with me as my Chaplain, and I am very much pleased, as all here are, with his conversation: After He had preached at Wigton, he went to his Parish where he stayed over Whitsunday; but the next morning came hither with Intenc~ons (I suppose) to continue with us. About 3 days after, Mr Weber (of whom I prsume you have heard) came also hither, in company of Mr Musgrave & another (younger) son of Sr Richard's from Hayton-Castle. I have entertained him likewise as my Chaplain, as I was before resolved to do, which will make the
busienesse more easy to them & to me too; being exceedingly well satisfied with them both.
My wife joins with me in ye Return of our best Respects & Services to your self & all yors at Ridal; and I am ever Worthy Sr,
ffor Sr Daniel Fleming Knight at Ridal This.

note.value: 744. DR. HENRY FLEMING TO SIR DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p:
Meeting last Thursday with the news of Mr Savage's death, I went that night to Penrith and yesterday morning to Rose in hopes
that the Bishop would have been as good as his word, and with desire of accepting of Caldbeck and quitting Grasmere: but I soon found that (contrary to truth and Honesty) Bro~. George was presented with the Prebendary, and Mr Wybergh with the living; so that I only told my mind a little to my Lord, (and came) home last night. Mr Wybergh must quit Lamp-(lieu so that) Brother Roger may probably get it with timely (application.)

(I found my) wife a little troubled with a sore breast which we (thought was) occasioned by cold, and wu'd soon mend; but last (night brought) me an account that it was burst. My Duty (and Ser)vice attends your self, my Brothers and Sisters, I am
For Sr Daniell Fleming att Rydal These.

note.value: 15. JOHN BANKES TO DANIEL FLEMING.

text.p: I would not willingly omit any Post but let you hear from Me wee have had not.

John And Mr Whartons to your father your Ante Anderton did show wh with the order to Mr Wales who is Clarke to the Comissionrs in Preston but he said the Comissionrs would take no notice off it unless the Auditor had either inserted the words we desired or write a l~re under his hand: which I could wish he had done ffor the Comissionrs are very Cautious of money the business is such a great arreare but I
hope by tomorrows Post wee shall receive the glad tidings of Allowance which indeed I shall be glad to see: yet before the original can be sued out I doe fear the will be very bussie with vs: yet if it pleasse god that we have Allowance or so granted it may be there might be some used with them to prevent them: Sr now our desire will be to resume the will or know where we may perceive it: ffor the Commission is to be executed at Preston the 22th of this Instant where the will would be very necessary. Sir your Mother is off opinion that if there any motions of peace by Crosland and Collingwood if wee get our Claim allowed it were ffit they wear embraced to prevent ffuture inconveniences: Sir my young Son is so extreme sick this night that I doe believe if he continue the lord that gave him will take him to his mercy: But I doe freely resign him to him that gave him.

Sir your Ante Dudley hath been sroke but is pretty well recovered All friends in that country are well. I have sent you herein enlossed
theise from your Uncle Hudleston which he desires that you will be pleased to take notice off. Some monies which you have disbursed ffor him might be repaid again by your ffather out off the 5l~ your Uncle left you at London. Your ffather mother brothers and sister here are all well. My wife presents her respects to you. Thus wishing Sir all health and happiness I rest as I am obliged
Your faithful Servant in all obedience John Banks Coniston this 8th Apprill 1653.
This ffor his ever honoured Moister Danyell fleming Esq at his Chamber at the Princes Arms in ffullers Rents near Greys Inn London these left I pray
